decisions.node_type: override fun m() in a class whose supertype declares m in the same file (K2/K34/K4 cluster)
decisions.question: Review K2: overrides carried no signature and every override was a first-parent guess at 0.5 even when the declaring parent was IN THIS FILE (weakest override machinery in the JVM family). What is the verification contract?
decisions.decision: In-file BFS verification (family convention: java JD-anon / scala waves): hoist a name-keyed declSigs index (owner -> method name -> Set<(T1,T2)>) ONCE (O(M), java C11 lesson). The FIRST ancestor in declaration order that declared a method WITH THE SAME NAME and a compatible signature verifies the edge at 0.9 / structural / reasonCode in-file-verified. The NAME dimension is load-bearing: name-blind sig membership fabricated cross-member overrides on the corpus (kotlinx-coroutines BroadcastChannel.kt: SubBroadcastChannel.send verified against BroadcastChannel which declares only cancel/sendSuspend - send comes from external SendChannel; 8 fabricated 0.9 edges at @200). Generic-substituted sigs (type-variable tokens) fall back to name-only pairing (scala SCD-E ruling). Parents that never declared the method keep the honest guess: 0.5 / inferred / first-supertype-guess (M37.10 family convention, below the 0.7 consumer threshold - K34 pin).

decisions.question: Review K4: override edges carry no signature, so overloads collapse and downstream cannot distinguish targets. Should the signature live in the edge source?
decisions.decision: Family convention (scala L433 / java C3): override sources stay Owner.name -> Parent.name - NO signature in the source string. The signature rides in metadata.overrideSig as a normalized '(T1,T2)' parameter-type list. Pinned by override-fallback-confidence (meta.overrideSig='()' + a forbid asserting the sig never leaks into the source) and the K4 claim-probe re-pin. Regression mutants: override-verification-downgrade (guess tier) and override-sig-payload-drop (payload loss) both die on the fixture.

decisions.question: Which spellings of a parameter type count as a TYPE VARIABLE for the generic-substitution fallback, given that the judge's rule (differential hasTypeVar, sigCompatible) and the analyzer's mirror must agree or the differential stops measuring one question?
decisions.decision: MIRROR THE JUDGE, BOUNDARY FOR BOUNDARY (the java #904 and scala S1.17 convention): a type variable is a SINGLE capital at `(`, `,`, `:`, `|`, `[`, `<`, `&` or string start — so `(T?)` is generic, and `(Byte?)`/`(Wrapped?)` are concrete. The nullable marker is stripped by the SCAN (the identifier ends at `?`), never by a per-token rule that would also make a nullable concrete type generic; the judge cannot derive an edge it reads as concrete, so widening past it fabricates UNEXPLAINED rows instead of fixing them. `kotlinSigHasTypeVar` is the third module-local copy of this scan (java javaSigHasTypeVar, scala sigHasTypeVar); consolidation into one shared mirror is a candidate, deliberately NOT taken in this round because two of the three lanes' rows are certified against their current bytes.

decisions.question: The F8 census injects ERROR and MISSING into every language's node-type set by hand (they are not in the wasm symbol table), yet no kotlin spec row claimed them, so section-a failed for kotlin on the same pair that fails lanes everywhere. Gap, silent omission, or handled?
decisions.decision: RULED — HANDLED, following the precedent the gate itself names and the java lane's own ruling (JDJ-2). The analyzer holds an EXPLICIT guard at real-kotlin-analyzer.ts:153 — `if (node.type === "ERROR" || node.type === "MISSING")` — which records a diagnostic and bypasses the damaged subtree. So ERROR is handled_verified and MISSING is internal_silent, the same split java, bash and javascript use. The guard being present is what makes the row CORRECT rather than grammar drift: a spec that classifies a node the analyzer consults was being told its own row was wrong, and the fix is never to delete the correct row.
decisions.evidence: Probed on the pinned grammar, 7 malformed inputs: `class E { class Inner { val w = 1 }` (unterminated class), `class F { val a = 1` (unterminated brace), `class H { val a = 1 } }` (stray close brace), `fun f(` (truncated parameter list), `val x =` (lone operator), `class I<T extends> { val a: List<,> }` (malformed generics), and a well-typed class with one bad method. Result in EVERY case: exactly 1 ERROR node, 0 MISSING nodes, hasError=true, and exactly 1 diagnostic ("Syntax ERROR detected. The Brain Engine is bypassing this broken node."). Partial extraction is preserved where the grammar recovered it — symbols were [w], [a], [H,a], [], [], [I,a], [ok] — so the guard bypasses the damaged node and not the file.
decisions.misssing_note: MISSING is internal_silent on a stronger ground than java's: the pinned kotlin grammar did not produce a single MISSING node across all 7 probes — it recovers to an ERROR node in every case — so the MISSING branch of the guard is unexercisable on this grammar rather than merely unexercised. The row is kept because the guard tests for it, and a guard branch that cannot currently be reached is still a statement about the analyzer's contract.

decisions.question: The override resolver has three passes: an in-file BFS that verifies the declarer by signature (0.9, in-file-verified), a companion-index variant of the same BFS (0.9, companion-index), and a fallback that names the FIRST SUPERTYPE at confidence 0.5 with reasonCode first-supertype-guess and evidenceClass inferred. Pass 3 fires when the declaring ancestor lives in another compilation unit and is therefore unknowable from this file alone. The justification in the code is that 0.5 sits BELOW THE CONSUMER THRESHOLD, so those rows read as declared suspicion rather than counted relationships. Is that justification sufficient, and what is the tier's actual error rate?
decisions.decision: RULED — the tier STAYS, and its justification is REPLACED by a measurement. Same ruling and same shape as java's JDJ-1, reached the same way: the reasoning was true but unquantified, which is not the same as verified. Measured on Exposed (250-file draw, every edge checked against a repo-wide index of types and their declared members built from all 791 .kt files): guess tier 302 edges — 105 correct, 197 WRONG = 65.2%; verified tier 103 edges — 103 correct, 0 wrong = 0.0%. Kotlin's guess tier is more than twice java's measured 30.6%.
decisions.why_it_stays: It is right about a third of the time, so suppressing it would delete 105 correct edges. Deleting a correct edge to avoid 197 wrong ones, at a confidence the code already labels `inferred` and carries a `reasonCode` for, is a worse trade than publishing both honestly — the consumer's decision to filter is better made by the consumer than made silently here.
decisions.what_the_measurement_changes: The JUSTIFICATION, which does not hold as written. The 0.7 `confidenceThreshold` in src/ast/patterns.ts is the default for ORPHANED-PATTERN DETECTION, not a filter on the relationship ingest path, and no confidence predicate was found on that path. So the tier's defensibility does not rest on a filter that might not exist; it rests on `reasonCode: first-supertype-guess` and `evidenceClass: inferred` being present on every row. That is why kotlin/override-guess-tier pins both rather than leaving them implied — a consumer must be able to distinguish a guess from a verified edge without hard-coding 0.5 as a magic number. Stated as unverified rather than refuted: the insert path was not located, so the claim that no filter exists is the absence of evidence found, not proof of absence.
decisions.comparability: Kotlin's 65.2% and java's 30.6% are NOT the same measurement. Java's denominator excluded 33 unverifiable guesses whose claimed owner was itself outside the repo, and reported 30.6% of the VERIFIABLE subset. This measurement has no unverifiable bucket: every claimed parent resolved to a type in the repo, and 0 were 'not a type at all'. So the two figures answer different questions and the difference is not only that kotlin is worse.
decisions.measurement_instrument: Three instrument versions, each of which produced a confidently wrong rate, and the sequence is the finding as much as the number: 79.1% when the index missed constructor-invocation supertypes (the dominant kotlin form, `class Column<T>(...) : ExpressionWithColumnType<T>()` — it found 2 of Column's 3); 66.2% when it also missed anonymous objects as types, so every anonymous_LazySizedIterable.* edge resolved to no hierarchy and scored wrong; 65.2% with the instrument validated. A rate is only as good as what the instrument can see, and an unvalidated instrument does not report uncertainty — it reports a number.
decisions.fixture: kotlin/override-guess-tier — 2 expects, 2 forbids. Disabling pass 3 fails the guess row. Disabling pass 1 does NOT remove the verified row: it SILENTLY DEMOTES it from 0.9/in-file-verified/structural to 0.5/first-supertype-guess/inferred, and the edge's presence is unchanged. That is the most dangerous available failure mode for this rule — a count-based check, a coverage number, and an existence assertion all pass — and it is why the fixture pins confidence, reasonCode and evidenceClass together. The forbids are the second load-bearing half: without the `override` modifier neither tier may fire, because guessing there fabricates an override that is really an overload.

decisions.node_type: method_declaration (first-supertype-guess: is the tier improvable per-file?)
decisions.question: KDJ-1 measured the guess tier at 65.2% wrong and kept it. The obvious follow-up is whether a BETTER per-file rule exists. The tier names supers[0]; the alternatives are supers[last], or preferring the supertype written as a constructor call (`Base()`, a class) over a bare one (`Repo`, an interface), on the theory that the declaring ancestor is more often a class. Is any per-file strategy better than supers[0]?
decisions.decision: RULED — NO. supers[0] is the best per-file strategy available, on BOTH corpora. Every alternative tested ties or regresses, so the tier is not improvable without cross-file knowledge, and the correct disposition is the one KDJ-1 already reached: keep it, label it, measure it. This is a measured NEGATIVE result and it closes the 'should we improve the tier' question rather than leaving it open.
decisions.measured: Exposed (791 .kt files, 1315 types, 6428 members; 302 guess edges): supers[0] 50.5% of the 208 verifiable; supers[last] 37.5%; prefer-first-ctor-called 50.5% (identical, +0). kotlinx-coroutines (1039 .kt, 1129 types, 6605 members; 272 guess edges): supers[0] 55.1% of 138 verifiable; supers[last] 26.1%; prefer-first-ctor-called 53.6% (a REGRESSION, -2).
decisions.why_no_strategy_can_win: Of the knowable rows, the declarer is at a DIFFERENT ancestor in roughly half — 102 of 208 on Exposed — and supers[0] cannot reach it, because per-file information contains the supertype NAMES and not their members. The analyzer's typeIndex is built from the current file's own symbols, so an out-of-file ancestor is invisible to it by construction. The remaining signal available per file is the position in the supertype list, and position 0 is the best of the positions tested. Anything smarter would need cross-file knowledge the per-file analyzer does not have, and the one available proxy — a member NAME heuristic — is exactly what KAD-MR3 K6 deleted from this analyzer (performKotlinTypeInference) for fabricating return types from name prefixes.
decisions.the_instrument_fourth_time: Two of my candidate strategies produced DEGENERATE metrics and that is what exposed the bug: prefer-first-ctor-called came out EXACTLY equal to supers[0] to the row, and 'rows with no constructor-call supertype' came out 0. The cause was marking every supertype as a constructor call because `Base()` and a bare `Repo` BOTH parse as a `delegation_specifier`; the real discriminator is a `constructor_invocation` CHILD, probed. With that fixed the finding REVERSED — the declarer is a bare/interface supertype in 38% of knowable rows and a class in only 20%, the opposite of what the broken flag reported. Fourth instrument bug of this review, and the second time a candidate IMPROVEMENT was an artefact of the instrument rather than a property of the analyzer.
decisions.corrects_kdj_1: KDJ-1's headline of 65.2% counts rows whose declarer is OUTSIDE the repo as wrong, because no declarer can be found. Those rows are unverifiable rather than known-bad: 92 of 302 on Exposed (30.5%) and 132 of 272 on kotlinx-coroutines (48.5%). java's JDJ-1 EXCLUDED its 33 unverifiable guesses and reported 30.6% of the verifiable subset, so the apples-to-apples figures are 49.5% wrong on Exposed (105 of 208 correct) and 44.9% wrong on kotlinx-coroutines (76 of 138 correct). Kotlin is still materially worse than java's 30.6%, but 65.2% overstates it by counting the unverifiable bucket as failure, and the earlier note saying only that 'the two are not comparable without saying so' should have led with the comparable number instead.

decisions.question: A class publishes `contains X -> X`: the class contains itself, because a primary constructor publishes a symbol NAMED AFTER THE CLASS and owned by it (`Money[constructor|owner=Money]`). A self-referential containment is either a naming collision or a real member, and the two readings imply different fixes: if it is a collision, the constructor should publish a distinct name so the edge reads `X -> X.constructor`; if it is real, the edge is correct and only looks odd. This review DERIVED the row into the contains oracle (so it is compared rather than sitting unexplained) and did NOT decide it, because the choice is a published-name-surface convention rather than a correctness question, and changing a published name is a consumer-visible break.
decisions.status_note: Recorded because the commit that introduced the derivation asserted it was 'recorded in the review rather than decided here', and at the time it was recorded NOWHERE — not in the review, not in the spec. The master review's claim audit found that. An unrecorded open question is indistinguishable from a decision, which is the failure mode the review format exists to prevent.
decisions.evidence: Measured: on a 96-file sample the pattern appears for every class that declares a primary constructor, so it is common rather than exceptional. The contains oracle emits it deliberately and the analyzer's `contains` tier publishes it, so the two agree and the row is covered — nothing is broken today. What is unresolved is whether the published SHAPE is the right one.
decisions.options: (a) Leave it: `X contains X` reads as 'the class holds its own constructor', which is defensible and costs nothing. (b) Publish the constructor under a distinct name, making the edge unambiguous — consumer-visible, and it would change every existing `X -> X` row in the store. (c) Suppress the containment and represent the constructor only as a symbol, which loses the fact that a class holds a constructor at all.
decisions.why_not_decided_here: All three options are defensible and the choice belongs to whoever owns the published name surface, not to a lane review that found the question while building an oracle. The important property — that the row is now COMPARED rather than silently absent — is achieved either way.

decisions.question: The master review probed Android-idiomatic constructs and found that a class or interface whose body opens and closes on a SINGLE LINE fails to parse: `class V { val y = 1 }` sets hasError with no ERROR and no MISSING node anywhere below it. The identical source with newlines — `class V {\n  val y = 1\n}` — parses clean. Is this an analyzer defect?
decisions.decision: RULED — a PINNED-GRAMMAR limitation, not an analyzer defect, and disclosed. The scope is narrow and was measured rather than assumed: it is exactly `class` and `interface` bodies on one line. `object O { val y = 1 }` is CLEAN, `enum class G { A, B }` is CLEAN, `fun f() { val a = 1 }` is CLEAN, and `data class P(val x: Int)` (no body) is CLEAN. So the earlier framing of this lane's grammar gap as 'nested classes do not parse' was too narrow — this is a second, independent, and more mechanically-triggered limitation.
decisions.why_it_never_showed_up: Both corpora and every kotlin fixture in this repo are newline-formatted, which is the ktlint/IDE convention, so the production is never exercised. Measured impact: 0 of the 1,830 corpus .kt files hit this shape, and 0 of the 49 kotlin fixtures do either. It is therefore a LATENT risk, not a live bug: a future one-line class fixture would parse as an error and silently assert nothing.
decisions.consequence_for_future_work: Two things follow. A fixture written with a one-line class body would be vacuous or fail confusingly, and any compact or GENERATED kotlin (minified output, code generators, doc examples) would fail wholesale rather than partially. Neither is fixable without rebuilding the wasm, which invalidates the grammar pin — the same release-basis decision as the nested-class limitation in the review.
decisions.how_it_was_found: By probing Android-idiomatic constructs rather than by inspecting the corpus. The probe's first result — receiver-scope chains apparently failing — was a FALSE POSITIVE caused by a control that also failed: `class V { fun f() { } }` errored, which is absurd for real code. Following the control down is what found the actual rule, and had the control not been run the finding would have been reported as 'receiver scopes are broken', which is wrong.

label_coverage._description: Which relationship labels this lane actually COMPARES, and which admitted labels have no oracle behind them. Measured by script/m14/verify-label-coverage.ts and script/m14/verify-truth-existence.ts. UPDATED by the M14 ontology wave (analyzer/DERIV_OVERRIDES): `imports` and `exports` were absent from the emitted set entirely, so they appear in declared_gaps below as ORACLE-UNREGISTERED rather than as silent omissions — the lane emits them (2,463 and 37 edges on a 120-file draw) and the shared differential cannot compare them until its owner registers script/m14/oracles/kotlin-module-edges.ts.

declared_gaps.label: imports
declared_gaps.reason: M14 ontology wave (DERIV_OVERRIDES): the analyzer emits 2,463 `imports` edges across 117 of 120 corpus files (one per import_header, source = the compilation unit, target = the path as written). The lane-owned truth derivation is written and unit-checked — script/m14/oracles/kotlin-module-edges.ts, 3,627 truth rows over a 200-file draw with 0 missing and 0 confident-unmatched — but it is NOT registered in script/m14/differential.ts, which is the master's file. Until it is, the differential's allowlist drops the label from the analyzer side and no truth derives it, so every edge is compared against nothing. Declared rather than left silent: an undeclared gap is the failure verify-label-coverage exists to produce.
declared_gaps.closes_when: the master adds the import to differential.ts, pushes deriveKotlinModuleEdges, and admits `imports` in the kotlin allowlist arm

declared_gaps.label: exports
declared_gaps.reason: M14 ontology wave (DERIV_OVERRIDES): the analyzer emits 37 `exports` edges across 17 of 120 corpus files (one per top-level declaration carrying neither `private` nor `internal`, source = the compilation unit). Same oracle file, same registration gap, same reason. The predicate is SHARED with the symbol-level ExportInfo array, so the two surfaces cannot disagree.
declared_gaps.closes_when: the master registers kotlin-module-edges and admits `exports` in the kotlin allowlist arm

declared_no_truth.label: overrides
declared_no_truth.reason: CORRECTED 2026-10-04 by the M14 ontology wave (analyzer/DERIV_OVERRIDES). This entry previously said 'this lane has no overrides oracle, so every analyzer overrides row enters the comparison with no truth to meet and is counted as an unexplained FABRICATION'. BOTH clauses were measurably false and the entry is replaced by the measurement: (1) deriveTreeEdges (differential.ts:19560) DOES derive kotlin override truth — 26 truth rows on one 200-file draw, all 26 covered, MISSING=0, and the harness's own COMPARED-WITH-NO-TRUTH line never fired; (2) the 122 comparable-but-unmatched rows are not fabrications — they carry confidence 0.5 with evidenceClass=inferred and reasonCode=first-supertype-guess, which the harness files as HEURISTIC. The gap this entry describes is real but it is a DIFFERENT one and it is now measured: the truth derivation indexes function_declaration members only, so the 1,837 `override val`/`override var` declarations per 200-file draw were invisible to BOTH sides. The analyzer now emits them (1,850 overrides edges on a 120-file draw, 13 in-file-verified) and script/m14/oracles/kotlin-overrides.ts derives their in-file-verified subset (13 truth rows on the same 200-file draw, 0 missing) — unregistered, which is why 11 UNEXPLAINED overrides rows appear on that draw until the master wires it.
declared_no_truth.closes_when: the master registers oracles/kotlin-overrides.ts, or extends deriveTreeEdges to index property_declaration members (the cheaper fix — it is the same collector, one node type)
